other_side: Zitron is not writing about politics at all, which is rather the point: his most recent substantial piece argues that the thing Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are busy negotiating over may not get built. His case is that essentially all the demand sits with two loss-making labs, that stripping OpenAI out of Microsoft's numbers leaves roughly $10.33bn of genuine third-party AI revenue, and that on the best reading the whole industry has about $110 billion of annual demand against 190 gigawatts of planned capacity needing trillions to fill. "If Microsoft doesn't have the demand, nobody has the demand," he writes. On that account the backlash is arguing about the siting of buildings whose financing, not their permits, is the binding constraint.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is whether the announced data-centre buildout actually gets built and paid for. Both accept as fact that construction plans have run far ahead of what third parties are currently paying for, and that the opposition is now genuinely bipartisan. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the gigawatts in planning convert into energised, revenue-bearing capacity, and the observable that settles it is the share of announced projects reaching commissioning on schedule, and who signs the offtake. The residue is pure worldview: Whittemore treats the buildout as a fact to be governed well, Zitron as a financing structure that collapses before governance matters. Whittemore is vindicated if criteria-based orders like Shapiro's are met and projects proceed under them; Zitron if quiet cancellations outrun the permits. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: almost nobody outside the two labs is paying for this yet. Watch cancellations against permit grants.
